objects.description_en: The merged-mesh, open-lid centrifuge used by the optimized opposite-slot loading protocol. This is distinct from the legacy centrifuge model used by ordinary tasks.
The converted CAD 3 × 4 rack used by rack placement recall v4, including its stepped guide geometry. Not the legacy horizontal tube-rack proxy.
The converted capped centrifuge tube used by rack recall v4; cap appearance and task placement are configured by the task instance.
The actual runtime-authored load-cell platform, tray and segmented display used by the optimized feedback weighing task. Preview exported from the task scene builder, not the legacy balance model.
The 10 g, 20 g, 50 g and 100 g weights with graspable necks and mass labels authored by the optimized weighing task. All four are shown together at their actual relative dimensions.
The capped cylindrical sample load used in the optimized weighing scene, exported directly from the same object authoring function used for collection and evaluation.
A transparent vessel used across grasping, pouring, mixing and device-operation tasks.
A conical laboratory vessel used as a manipulation target and scene object.
A small sample container used in transport, organization and autosampler workflows.
A rigid laboratory tube used for rack insertion, transport and reset tasks.
A slender tube for high-precision insertion into an NMR autosampler rack.
A capped tube loaded into symmetric centrifuge rotor slots.
The rigid manipulation proxy used with a structured two-stop plunger and scalar liquid-volume state for aspiration and dispensing.
The indexed fixture proxy used to represent disposable-tip installation state during pipetting tasks.
A simplified labelled 2×2 plate proxy with scalar per-well volumes for recipe-based dispensing.
A labelled multi-socket rack for tube insertion and placement.
A numbered rack for precise NMR tube insertion and visual slot reasoning.
A compartmented fixture for vial transport, cohort organization and sorting.
A rigid disposal-target proxy used to verify that a pipette tip is discarded after liquid transfer.
A six-position rotor supporting symmetric loading and slot-reasoning tasks.
A digital balance used for structured mass reading and weight-selection workflows.
A physical mass display and four-choice control panel used to evaluate visually grounded digital reading.
A laboratory status display with Wait and Open controls for threshold- and state-dependent decisions.
A digital rotational-speed interface with increase, confirm and decrease controls.
A labelled 10 g, 20 g, 50 g and 100 g rigid weight set.
A lidded device with rotor and controls for loading and preset-operation tasks.
A lidded programmable device used for door, sample and button-operation sequences.
A programmable heating fixture for load-run-retrieve and temperature reasoning tasks.
Device-integrated Start, Wait, Open and Close controls used for state-dependent laboratory operation.
A slender tool used for controlled stirring in a laboratory vessel.

site.description: Evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions.

paper.abstract: Realizing Embodied AI for Science requires robots to translate experimental goals into reliable physical procedures, reducing hazardous and repetitive human work while generating evidence for scientific discovery. Although language-based planning and learned manipulation provide complementary capabilities, their integration requires robots to adapt subsequent operations to actual execution outcomes. For example, an unsuccessful placement changes what must be done next, even when the experimental goal remains unchanged. Existing benchmarks assess planning, manipulation, and laboratory workflows through task completion and reasoning or execution metrics; however, aggregate performance leaves the connection between outcome-dependent choices and physical execution unresolved. To address this evaluation gap, we introduce Labference, a benchmark for evaluating how observed physical outcomes guide subsequent choices and how those choices translate into robotic laboratory actions. Its evaluation protocol is designed to test outcome-dependent behavioral adaptation through controlled evidence variations, while independently measuring operation selection, physical execution, and task completion. Matched Oracle-assisted continuations from shared checkpoints then assess which forms of support improve subsequent choices and task completion. Initial weighing evaluations reveal target-selection errors in the tested VLA policies despite successful object transfers, whereas GPT-driven control achieves correct selection but encounters execution failures and substantial computation costs. Together, these findings highlight the need to connect task-appropriate reasoning with reliable, timely action. By making this connection measurable and diagnosable, Labference supports targeted improvements toward autonomous experimentation for Embodied AI for Science.
paper.title: Labference: Benchmarking the Reasoning–Action Connection in Robotic Laboratories
